opus-5.5.text:
I think there will be some specialization, but probably less than people expect, at least in the near term. Historically, a lot of robotics has looked like that: you design a very specific machine for a very specific task, like a robot that only picks one kind of part off a conveyor, and it works well in that narrow setting. The problem is that each of those systems is expensive to design, and it doesn't transfer. You can't take what you learned from it and apply it anywhere else.

What we've been seeing with learning-based approaches is that if you can collect data across many different robots and many different tasks, the models actually get better. A model trained on lots of different embodiments often does better on a given robot than one trained only on that robot's data. That pushes you toward fairly general-purpose hardware, something like arms with reasonably capable grippers, maybe on a mobile base, that can do many things, rather than a bespoke machine per use case.

That said, I don't think hardware is going to collapse to a single form factor. There are settings where the economics or physical constraints really favor something specialized. If you need extreme speed, a particular payload, or you're working in a very constrained environment, a custom design will make sense. And I think there's also going to be a middle ground where you have a fairly general platform with different end effectors or attachments for different domains.

My bet is that the intelligence, the software and the models, ends up being shared and general, and the hardware becomes somewhat more modular and cheaper over time. The more the model can compensate for imperfect or low-cost hardware, the less you need to specialize the hardware itself. That's a big part of what makes this moment exciting: if the brain is general enough, you don't need to reinvent the body for every new task.

r001.rationale: The response says specialized systems can be expensive to design and that hardware may become cheaper over time, but it does not say use-case optimization can lower hardware cost.

r002.rationale: The response says extreme speed can make a custom design worthwhile, but does not clearly state that specializing hardware can make it substantially faster.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think it's quite plausible, and honestly I think we're already partway there. If you look at robotics specifically, the hardware and the model are not really separable the way they are in, say, language. The robot is the interface to the world, and the data you collect is shaped by what that body can do. So if you want a robot that's really good at folding laundry or doing dishes in a home, you probably don't want a 200-pound industrial arm. You want something that's cheap, compliant, safe around people, and has the right kind of hand for manipulating deformable objects. That's a different design point from something you'd deploy in a warehouse moving boxes all day.

That said, I'd push back a little on how far specialization goes. One of the big lessons from the last few years is that general-purpose models trained on diverse data tend to win over narrow ones, and I think that applies to the policy side even if the hardware varies. So my guess is the future looks like a fairly small number of general foundation models, trained across many embodiments, that then get deployed on hardware that is specialized for a use case. The specialization lives more in the body and the sensors than in the brain.

There's also a practical argument. Robots are expensive, and the economics only work if you can amortize the cost over something people actually want done repeatedly. So the first successful deployments will almost certainly be use-case driven, and the hardware will be optimized around that. I'd be surprised if the first robot in most people's homes were a fully humanoid generalist. It's more likely to be something narrower that does one or two things well, and the generality comes later, once the software has caught up.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a costly industrial arm with use case specific hardware described as cheap, linking specialization to lower cost.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that use case specific hardware could make a robot substantially faster.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s pretty plausible. If you know exactly what you want a robot to do, you can design the hardware around that task, and that can make the problem a lot easier. You don’t necessarily need a humanoid to move things around a warehouse.

The tradeoff is flexibility. If the task changes, or you want that robot to do something else, specialized hardware can become a limitation. So I’d expect a mix: hardware that’s specialized for particular environments or tasks, but software that shares a lot across those different robots. You could have fairly general intelligence running on bodies that look quite different.

r001.rationale: The response says task-specific hardware can make the problem easier, but it does not state that it can make hardware cheaper.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest that task-specific hardware could make the system substantially faster.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s pretty plausible. If you know exactly what you want a robot to do, you can design the hardware around that task, and that can make the learning problem a lot easier. You don’t necessarily need a hand with five fingers to pick something up; a simple gripper might work really well.

The tradeoff is flexibility. If you want a robot that can do lots of different things in a home, it’s harder to specialize the hardware because the tasks and environments vary so much. So I could imagine a future with fairly general-purpose software running on a range of different bodies, some designed for particular applications and some designed to be more versatile.
